Since every entry of a matrix-vector or matrix-matrix product is just a sum of column products, you don't need real linear algebra support in Polars: generate the sum-of-products expressions programmatically and let the streaming engine treat them like any other expression. Represent M as a nested list of column-name strings and v as a list of column names, then build one expression per output using pl.sum_horizontal:

def matvec(M, v, out_names):
    return [pl.sum_horizontal([pl.col(M[i][j]) * pl.col(v[j]) for j in range(len(v))]).alias(out_names[i]) for i in range(len(M))]

lf.with_columns(matvec(M, v, ["v1","v2","v3"]))

This is pure Python building an expression list, so it composes fine with lazy/streaming execution. For chained multiplications, feed one stage's output column names in as the next stage's v, or symbolically multiply two nested lists of expressions before calling with_columns once. Wrap this in a small helper keyed by matrix shape and you get automatic expansion without ever materializing more than the streaming engine already batches.

BashOperator's do_xcom_push only captures the single last line written to the command's stdout; that exact string becomes the XCom value, nothing else. Check: (1) myscript.py must end with a bare print(value), not logging (which usually goes to stderr and isn't captured), as the very last thing it outputs, any later print/debug/warning line or trailing blank line will overwrite or blank out what gets pushed; (2) the task must exit 0 for XCom to be recorded; (3) run the exact bash_command manually and confirm the last stdout line is exactly what you expect. Also verify the f-string in your bash_command isn't mangling anything unexpected. Then inspect Admin > XComs in the Airflow UI for that specific first_status task instance to see the literal value stored; if it's empty or None, the problem is entirely in what myscript.py prints to stdout, not in how the second BashOperator's Jinja template pulls it.

Two likely causes. First, your custom coverage bool_flag and Bazel's native collect_code_coverage/instrumentation_filter are independent mechanisms; your select() only adds -fprofile-arcs/-ftest-coverage compiler flags to targets that explicitly use your wrapper macro. If any cc_library in the dependency chain doesn't route through that same wrapper, its objects compile without --coverage and produce no gcno, even though sibling files in a library that does use the wrapper get instrumented. Audit every cc_library/cc_binary between your binary and the file missing gcno to confirm all of them apply the wrapper's copts/linkopts. Second, instrumentation_filter="^//src[/:]" matches by target label/package; files living in a different package, an external repo, or generated under bazel-out won't be instrumented by Bazel's native bookkeeping regardless of your manual copts. Check the exact label of the affected files against that regex. bazel query 'deps(//your:binary)' --output=label_kind, cross-checked against each target's copts, is the fastest way to find the target missing the wrapper.

This is a known limitation of ExpectColumnValuesToBeIncreasing (and Decreasing) against datetime64 columns in current Great Expectations: internally the metric computes successive differences, which come back as pandas Timedelta, and compares them against a plain int threshold (0), causing the ">=" not supported between Timedelta and int error. It works for null/unique/regex expectations because those don't do numeric or temporal comparisons. Workaround: don't validate the raw datetime column directly; convert it to an integer representation first, e.g. df["Date"] = df["Date"].astype("int64") for nanosecond timestamps, or map to ordinal via pd.Timestamp.toordinal, and run ExpectColumnValuesToBeIncreasing against that numeric column instead. Also check the Great Expectations GitHub issues for this expectation plus datetime columns; it has been reported before, so upgrading or downgrading your great_expectations version may already resolve it. If you need to keep the original Date column for other checks, just add the int-cast version as an extra column in the same dataframe purely for this one expectation.

A couple of likely issues. First, in TexStudio's scripting API editor is a function, not a property; you need editor().insertText(output), not editor.insertText(output). Using it without calling it can silently target the wrong place, consistent with your output landing in the Messages panel instead of the document. Second, proc.standardOutput may need explicit string conversion in your Qt/TexStudio version; try var output = ""+proc.standardOutput, or read via proc.readAllStandardOutput() depending on version. Third, clean up what Python prints: repr(str(fn)+"xxxx") wraps the string in quotes and escape characters, which is almost certainly not the literal includegraphics text you want inserted; print the raw string with print(result, end="") (no repr, no trailing newline) so output is exactly the text to insert. Test incrementally: alert(typeof output) and alert(output.length) first, to confirm the process actually returned something before troubleshooting insertText's target further.

"failed to map segment from shared object" when loading a compiled .so under mod_wsgi on Fedora is the classic signature of SELinux blocking execmem/execmod for a shared library mmap'd by httpd. Fedora ships SELinux enforcing by default; Rocky 9's policy or your venv's file contexts apparently allow it while Fedora 42/43 don't, often because the venv was created or copied in a way that left it with the wrong context (e.g. user_tmp_t) instead of one httpd is allowed to execute from. Check sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent (or journalctl) for AVC denials around the time of the request; denials referencing httpd_t plus execmem/execmod confirm this. Fixes: relabel the venv with sudo restorecon -Rv /var/www/html/test/venv after ensuring the parent directory has a correct context, or more broadly sudo setsebool -P httpd_execmem 1. Also confirm the filesystem isn't mounted noexec. This is unrelated to your numpy version; any compiled extension loaded by mod_wsgi can trigger it.

This looks like a mismatch between the model's custom KV-cache handling code and the transformers version's Cache API, not a hyperparameter bug. Since transformers introduced Cache objects (e.g. DynamicCache) to replace the old tuple-of-tuples past_key_values, that cache starts empty until something calls cache.update(...); code written for the legacy format that indexes past_key_values[0] directly will hit exactly this "Cache only has 0 layers" error if nothing has populated layer 0, likely if RAMLLaMA's custom modeling code predates the Cache API changes between versions 4.35 and 4.44. Since you need >=4.43 for gamma2 but the RAMLLaMA/unsloth modeling code may not be updated for the newer Cache internals, the two requirements may genuinely conflict in your current combination. Check the RAMQA/unsloth repo's issues or changelog for a transformers version known to support gamma2 without this break, or patch the custom attention code to initialize past_key_values = DynamicCache() and call .update() instead of indexing it positionally. This likely needs an upstream code fix rather than a config change.

This is almost certainly the New Outlook, not Python 3.14 or pywin32. New Outlook is a rebuilt web-based client and does not implement the classic COM Automation server (Outlook.Application) the way desktop Outlook does; even with classic Outlook also installed, if New Outlook is the active one, COM activation can fail with exactly "Server execution failed" because the registered server behavior differs between the two. Fix: turn off "Try the New Outlook" (toggle in the top-right of Outlook) so classic Outlook is what's actually running, open it manually once, then retry win32com.client.Dispatch("Outlook.Application"). Also make sure your Python process and Outlook run at the same privilege/integrity level and in the same user session; COM activation commonly fails across an elevation or session boundary (e.g. script run as admin, Outlook run as normal user). Python 3.14 plus pywin32 isn't a known blocker for Outlook automation by itself, as long as pywin32 finished installing cleanly (rerun its post-install script if unsure).

Most likely cause: your build backend (hatchling, uv's default) determines included files from your VCS file list by default; if the j2 templates under src/mypackage/j2/ aren't tracked by git, they get silently excluded from the built wheel even though they exist on disk. Run git add on the template files first and check git status. If they're tracked and still missing, add an explicit include:

[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel]
packages = ["src/mypackage"]

[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel.force-include]
"src/mypackage/j2" = "mypackage/j2"

or add [tool.hatch.build] include = ["src/mypackage/j2/**"]. Separately, don't rely on relative filesystem paths to find templates at runtime since that breaks once installed as a wheel; use importlib.resources instead: importlib.resources.files("mypackage.j2").joinpath("template.j2").read_text(), or point Jinja2's PackageLoader("mypackage", "j2") at it, which is built exactly for this and works both from source checkouts and installed wheels.

This smells like a version difference in awslambdaric (the Lambda Runtime Interface Client) between AWS's own Python base images and whatever pip installs on plain Debian. AWS's managed images bundle a build with mature Function-URL response handling, correctly detecting the payload-format-2.0 shape (statusCode/headers/body/isBase64Encoded) and serializing it into an HTTP response, while an independently pip-installed awslambdaric can lag behind or handle that path differently, consistent with the console "Test" invoke (which just echoes any return value as raw JSON) succeeding while only the HTTP function-URL path fails on a dict return. Compare pip show awslambdaric's version against what AWS's base image ships, and try pinning to the latest release. Also double check your returned dict's keys and types exactly match {"statusCode": int, "headers": {...}, "body": str, "isBase64Encoded": bool}; function URLs are stricter about this than the Test tab. If pinning doesn't help, this is worth filing against the aws-lambda-python-runtime-interface-client repo directly.

If Matrix is a numpy array (wrap nested lists with np.array(Matrix) first), just slice it into quadrants:

import numpy as np
M = np.array(Matrix)
A = M[:2, :2]
B = M[:2, 2:]
C = M[2:, :2]
D = M[2:, 2:]

For splitting an n by n array into equal b by b blocks in general, reshape plus swapaxes does it in one shot:

n, b = M.shape[0], 2
blocks = M.reshape(n//b, b, n//b, b).swapaxes(1, 2)
# blocks[0,0]==A, blocks[0,1]==B, blocks[1,0]==C, blocks[1,1]==D

Or use np.split twice if you'd rather avoid reshape/swapaxes:

top, bottom = np.vsplit(M, 2)
A, B = np.hsplit(top, 2)
C, D = np.hsplit(bottom, 2)

Any of these work; direct slicing is simplest for one fixed known layout, reshape/swapaxes is nicer when you want all blocks generated programmatically for an arbitrary block size.

DataFrame.mad() and Series.mad() were deprecated in pandas 1.5 and removed in 2.0, so there's no direct replacement method in 2.1.4; pandas' own deprecation notice recommends computing it manually instead:

(df - df.mean()).abs().mean()

for a DataFrame column-wise, or for a Series:

(s - s.mean()).abs().mean()

If you actually want median absolute deviation rather than mean absolute deviation, use scipy: from scipy.stats import median_abs_deviation, then median_abs_deviation(df, axis=0); or in pandas terms, (df - df.median()).abs().median(). There's no plan to reintroduce mad() as a method, so the manual one-liner is the officially suggested replacement rather than a workaround, and it's safe to rely on going forward.

A 403 from requests and a blank Selenium page suggest more than a missing header; NYSCEF is a government e-filing system, and ViewDocument links typically require an authenticated session (cookies from the case-search flow) plus possibly bot-detection that blocks headless or non-browser clients outright. Try: (1) in Selenium, don't hit the PDF URL directly; first navigate to the NYSCEF search/case page, let it fully load so session cookies get set, then navigate to ViewDocument in the same browser context; (2) run non-headless with real waits for network idle, since the PDF may load asynchronously into an embed/iframe; inspect the network tab (or intercept requests in SeleniumBase) for the actual PDF byte-stream URL rather than assuming it's the page URL itself; (3) copy Selenium's cookies via driver.get_cookies() into a requests.Session with a matching User-Agent/Referer if you want a requests-based fallback afterward. If none of that works, the specific docket document may require a logged-in NYSCEF account with access to that case, not just a public link.

Technically yes; in Tkinter the master argument just needs to be any Tk widget, since every widget is backed by an actual window internally, and pack/grid/place only require a valid Tk window to attach children to. Tkinter doesn't restrict parenthood to Frame/Toplevel/Canvas at the C level; that's a convention, not an enforced rule. It's unsupported in practice, though: Label and Button aren't designed to manage child geometry, so results are inconsistent across platforms. You're seeing the Entry render inside the Button on Linux, but on Windows or macOS, which use more strictly themed widget rendering especially with ttk, the same code can clip children, ignore them, size oddly, or look broken, because those widgets don't reserve or manage internal layout space the way a Frame does. Stick to Frame, LabelFrame, Canvas, or Toplevel as containers for anything meant to hold child widgets, and treat this working on your Linux setup as non-portable rather than as confirmation it's a supported pattern.

The likely bug is your marker-count formula, not custom ids per se. A ChArUco board places markers only on alternating squares of the checkerboard, so the correct marker count for a squaresX by squaresY board is (squaresX*squaresY)//2, not (squaresX-1)*(squaresY-1) as you compute; for 11x8 that's 44 versus your 70. Passing an ids array of the wrong length, reshaped into a 2D grid on top of that, means OpenCV's C++ CharucoBoard constructor reads or writes past the bounds of the array it's given internally, a textbook segfault cause rather than something Python would catch as an exception. Fix: compute num_markers = (self.squaresX * self.squaresY) // 2, and pass a flat 1D array with no reshape:

marker_ids = np.arange(start_id, start_id + num_markers, dtype=np.int32)

Pass that 1D array directly as the ids argument. Also cross-check against the cv2.aruco documentation or examples for your exact 4.11.0 build, since the expected marker count and layout convention can vary slightly by board/marker variant.

mypy treats user-defined generic classes as invariant in their type parameters by default. Ok[Dog] is therefore not assignable to Ok[Animal] even though Dog is one arm of the Animal union; invariance means the type argument must match exactly, not merely be compatible. Marking T covariant would fix the return-type check, but your frozen dataclass still generates __init__(self, value: T), a parameter position, and mypy forbids a covariant TypeVar from appearing in any parameter position, even a synthesized one, because covariance is only sound when T appears solely in output positions. That's the contradiction: the type is read-only in spirit, but the generated constructor makes it look mutable to the checker. Practical fixes: narrow at each call site with an explicit cast, return cast(Result[Animal, str], decodeDog(slop)); or add a targeted type: ignore[return-value] comment on each delegating return; or avoid delegating directly and instead pattern-match the inner Ok/Err and rewrap it, e.g. match decodeDog(slop): case Ok(v): return Ok(v), case Err(e): return Err(e), which mypy accepts because Dog is directly assignable to Animal there.

No, this isn't possible today. PEP 646's TypeVarTuple only lets you pass *Ts through unchanged, or prepend/append fixed items around it, like tuple[int, *Ts], or bind it to another TypeVarTuple; there's no elementwise "map" operation defined in the type system to transform each element of the tuple, such as wrapping each in list[...], while staying generic over arbitrary arity. Neither the PEP nor current mypy or pyright implement anything like the tuple[list[T] for T in *Ts] syntax you're picturing, and there's no separate PEP currently proposing it. Practical workarounds: if you only need a handful of fixed arities, write explicit overloads for each, one returning tuple[list[T1]], another tuple[list[T1], list[T2]], and so on; or give up precision and type it as tuple[list[Any], ...]; or, if the elements are actually homogeneous, use a plain TypeVar with a regular variadic tuple or Sequence instead of TypeVarTuple, since that case never needed per-element mapping in the first place.

This is a name collision, not case-sensitivity in general. Q is a reserved name in sympy: sympy.Q is the assumptions query object (sympy.assumptions.ask.Q, used for things like Q.positive(x)), which lands in your namespace via from sympy import *. When you pass the string "Q" into solve(gf, "x", "Q", "y"), sympy has to sympify that string, and it resolves against sympy's own globals first; it finds the existing Q assumptions object instead of creating or matching an ordinary Symbol, so recast_to_symbols fails trying to sympify that AssumptionKeys object as though it were a plain symbol name, raising SympifyError. Lowercase "q" has no such collision, so it works fine. Fix: avoid the capital letter Q, renaming your symbol to q or Qval; or better, stop passing symbol names as bare strings altogether; create the Symbol explicitly with Q = symbols("Q") and pass that Symbol object to solve, solve(gf, x, Q, y), rather than the string "Q".

Two likely culprits. First, common needs to actually be installed into user-service's virtualenv for the common.tests.db_conf import to resolve at all; a shared monorepo folder layout alone isn't enough, so add it as a path or editable dependency in user-service's pyproject.toml so it lands on site-packages. Second, and easy to miss: pytest only reliably honors a pytest_plugins = [...] declaration by dotted path when it's defined in the rootdir's top-level conftest.py; declaring it in a non-root conftest.py, like user-service/tests/conftest.py, is deprecated and restricted in modern pytest versions and can silently fail to register the plugin. Move pytest_plugins = ["common.tests.db_conf"] to the actual root conftest.py of your test run, or better, turn common.tests.db_conf into a proper installable pytest plugin using a pytest11 entry point in common's pyproject.toml instead of relying on the dotted-path pytest_plugins mechanism across separate packages, the more robust pattern for shared fixtures across packages.

What you're seeing is expected, if confusing: style.configure() writes into Tk's style/resource database and echoes back whatever key or value you set, including arbitrary ones like text, but that doesn't mean every element actually reads that option when rendering. For Button.label, the displayed text comes from the individual widget's own -text option or -textvariable, not from the style database; each button obviously needs different text, so the style layer intentionally doesn't drive content that way, even though element_options() lists text as a technically settable option on that element. So style.configure("TButton", text=...) gets stored and returned by a later configure() call, but has no visual effect on existing or new Button widgets; it's effectively a no-op for content. Only genuinely visual options, background, foreground, font, padding, relief, anchor, and similar, are meaningfully themable this way. To set text, use button.config(text=...) or a textvariable on each instance directly instead of trying to drive it through the style system.
